blocks.content: Before WebSockets were everywhere, apps still felt live. Early Gmail chat and Facebook chat delivered messages the instant they arrived, using nothing but ordinary HTTP requests. The trick they used has a name: long polling.
The idea is simple and clever. The client asks the server for updates, but instead of answering immediately with nothing, the server keeps the request waiting until it actually has something to send.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396028628-51845736.png
blocks.alt: Long polling: the server holds the request open until data is ready

blocks.content: 1. What Long Polling Is
Long polling is a technique where the client sends a request and the server holds it open until new data is available, or until a timeout is reached, and only then responds.
The moment the client receives a response, it immediately sends another request. So there is nearly always a request parked on the server, ready to deliver the next update with no delay.

blocks.title: The one line version
blocks.content: Short polling asks again and again. Long polling asks once and waits, and the server answers the instant there is real news.
The easiest way to appreciate it is to compare it directly with short polling.
The clearest way to understand long polling is to watch it next to short polling.
Short polling asks on a fixed timer and mostly gets empty answers:
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785278407674-448624281.png
blocks.alt: Short polling: a request on a fixed timer, usually returning nothing

blocks.content: Long polling asks once, and the server simply does not answer until it has something:
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785278409325-320813065.png
blocks.alt: Long polling: the server holds the request, then answers instantly

blocks.content: The difference is night and day. Short polling produces a steady stream of empty responses and always lags by up to the interval. Long polling produces almost no empty responses and delivers updates nearly instantly.
["Short polling: fixed interval, many empty responses, delay up to the interval","Long polling: request held open, responses only when there is data, near instant delivery"]
items: Short polling: fixed interval, many empty responses, delay up to the interval
Long polling: request held open, responses only when there is data, near instant delivery

blocks.content: 2. How Long Polling Works, With Code
blocks.text: 2. How Long Polling Works, With Code

blocks.content: The full cycle is short and repeats forever.

["The client sends a request asking for anything new since its last update","The server checks for new data","If there is data, it responds right away","If there is none, it holds the request open and waits","When data arrives, or a timeout is reached, the server responds","The client processes the response and immediately sends the next request"]
items: The client sends a request asking for anything new since its last update
The server checks for new data
If there is data, it responds right away
If there is none, it holds the request open and waits
When data arrives, or a timeout is reached, the server responds
The client processes the response and immediately sends the next request

blocks.content: That last step is the heart of it. Because the client reconnects the instant it gets a reply, the server almost always has a live request to push the next update into.
Seeing the same cycle in code makes it concrete.
Here is the client. Notice how it calls itself again the moment a response returns.
And here is the server, holding the request until there is data or a timeout fires.

The timeout is not optional. Without it a request could hang forever and tie up resources. A common choice is to hold for about thirty seconds, then send an empty response so the client reconnects cleanly.
3. The Cursor and the Gap
There is a subtle problem. Between the moment the server responds and the moment the client reconnects, there is a tiny window with no live request. What if an event happens right then?
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785278410972-989942654.png
blocks.alt: A cursor closes the gap: the client asks for everything since its last id

blocks.content: The fix is a cursor. The client remembers the id or timestamp of the last update it saw, and asks for everything since that point. So even if an event lands during the gap, the very next request picks it up and nothing is lost.

blocks.title: Why the cursor matters
blocks.content: Without a cursor, long polling can silently drop any event that occurs in the gap between requests. The cursor turns a fragile design into a reliable one.
4. Timeouts and Reconnection
Long lived requests bump into a few realities of the network that you have to plan for.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785278412518-698729648.png
blocks.alt: On timeout the server returns empty and the client simply reconnects

blocks.content: ["Set a server side timeout, often twenty to sixty seconds, then respond empty so the client reconnects","Track a cursor so no updates are missed between requests","Handle failures on the client, since networks drop and requests can error out","Watch proxies and load balancers, which may cut idle connections earlier than your timeout"]
items: Set a server side timeout, often twenty to sixty seconds, then respond empty so the client reconnects
Track a cursor so no updates are missed between requests
Handle failures on the client, since networks drop and requests can error out
Watch proxies and load balancers, which may cut idle connections earlier than your timeout

blocks.content: 5. How the Server Waits Efficiently
A held request is waiting, but how does the server wake it the instant data is ready, without sitting in a busy loop hammering the database?

The clean pattern is to pair long polling with a publish subscribe system. The held request subscribes to a channel, for example the user inbox, and waits. When an event is published to that channel, the subscription fires, the request wakes, and the server responds at once.

["The request arrives and subscribes to the relevant channel","It waits without consuming a thread on an async server","A publisher sends an event to that channel","The waiting request wakes and responds with the data","A timeout still guards against waiting forever"]
items: The request arrives and subscribes to the relevant channel
It waits without consuming a thread on an async server
A publisher sends an event to that channel
The waiting request wakes and responds with the data
A timeout still guards against waiting forever

blocks.title: Why this matters
blocks.content: Polling the database in a loop for every held request would crush it. A pub sub wakeup means the server does nothing until there is real news, which is exactly what makes long polling efficient.
This waiting only stays cheap on the right kind of server.
The single biggest implementation detail is the server model, because long polling only scales on an event driven, non blocking server.
On a thread per request server, each held request occupies a whole thread doing nothing, so a few thousand waiting clients exhaust the pool and the server stops accepting work.
On an event driven server like Node, a held request is just a callback waiting on an event, costing almost nothing, so a single process can hold tens of thousands of connections at once.
6. A Worked Example: A Notification Bell
blocks.text: 6. A Worked Example: A Notification Bell

blocks.content: Picture the notification bell in a web app. You want the little red badge to appear the instant something happens, without running WebSockets.

["The browser opens a long poll request to the notifications endpoint with its last seen id","The server subscribes that request to the user notification channel and holds it","Someone comments on the user post, which publishes an event","The held request wakes, and the server responds with the new notification","The browser shows the badge and immediately reopens the request"]
items: The browser opens a long poll request to the notifications endpoint with its last seen id
The server subscribes that request to the user notification channel and holds it
Someone comments on the user post, which publishes an event
The held request wakes, and the server responds with the new notification
The browser shows the badge and immediately reopens the request

blocks.content: This is close to how many notification systems worked before WebSockets, and it still works today behind the strictest proxies.

blocks.title: The same pattern scales up
blocks.content: Swap the held HTTP request for a WebSocket and this exact design becomes a WebSocket notification system. The pub sub core stays the same, only the transport changes.
7. Advantages and Limitations
Long polling is loved for being simple and universal, but it is not free.

8. Long Polling vs SSE vs WebSockets
blocks.text: 8. Long Polling vs SSE vs WebSockets

blocks.content: Long polling is one point on a spectrum of real time techniques. Knowing where it sits tells you when to pick it.

{"headers":["Technique","Direction","Connection","Best for","Real examples"],"rows":[["Short polling","Client asks repeatedly","New request each time","Simple, infrequent updates","Basic status checks"],["Long polling","Client asks, server holds","Reopened after each response","Near real time on plain HTTP","Older Gmail and Facebook chat"],["SSE","Server to client only","One long lived connection","Live feeds and notifications","Stock tickers, live scores"],["WebSockets","Two way","One persistent connection","Chat, games, collaboration","WhatsApp, Slack, Figma"],["WebRTC","Peer to peer","Direct between clients","Audio and video","Zoom, Google Meet"]]}
Choose long polling when you need near real time on plain HTTP and cannot or do not want to run WebSocket servers. Move to SSE for one way streams, or WebSockets when both sides send heavily.
9. Scaling Long Polling
The core scaling fact is that every waiting client is holding an open request on the server the whole time it waits.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785278414621-175802754.png
blocks.alt: Many held connections need a non blocking, event driven server

blocks.content: On a traditional server that dedicates one thread per request, a few thousand waiting clients can exhaust the thread pool while doing nothing. This is why long polling needs an event driven model.

["Use non blocking, asynchronous servers like Node or Netty, so a held request costs almost nothing while it waits","Expect very high connection counts, since many clients wait at once","Use a shared store or broker so any server can answer with the latest data","Tune load balancer and proxy timeouts so they allow long lived requests"]
items: Use non blocking, asynchronous servers like Node or Netty, so a held request costs almost nothing while it waits
Expect very high connection counts, since many clients wait at once
Use a shared store or broker so any server can answer with the latest data
Tune load balancer and proxy timeouts so they allow long lived requests

blocks.content: The HTTP version you run also affects how well this scales.

A modern nuance is worth knowing. Over old HTTP/1.1, a browser allowed only a handful of connections per domain, and a held long poll used one of those slots, which could block other requests to the same site.
Over HTTP/2, many streams share one connection, so a held long poll no longer starves other requests. It does not make long polling more real time, but it removes a real old pain point.
10. Where Long Polling Is Used
Long polling carried real time features for years, and it still earns its place today.

["Early Gmail and Facebook chat, using a style once called Comet","Fallback transport in libraries like Socket.IO when WebSockets are blocked","Notification and alert systems","Live comment and activity feeds behind strict corporate proxies"]
items: Early Gmail and Facebook chat, using a style once called Comet
Fallback transport in libraries like Socket.IO when WebSockets are blocked
Notification and alert systems
Live comment and activity feeds behind strict corporate proxies

blocks.content: Its staying power comes from working everywhere. When WebSockets are blocked by an old proxy or firewall, long polling still gets through.
Its staying power is not an accident, it has a long history on the web.
Long polling and its cousins were popular enough in the 2000s to earn a nickname: Comet. It was the umbrella term for pushing data to the browser before WebSockets existed.
That history explains why long polling is so widely supported. It was the workhorse of real time on the early web, so every browser, proxy, and framework handles it well to this day.
In short, if a feature has to work for absolutely every user, on any network, behind any proxy, long polling is still the most compatible option available.
That is why many real time systems keep it as a fallback even after moving their main traffic to WebSockets.
11. Securing Long Polling
Because long polling rides on ordinary HTTP requests, it inherits the normal web security model, which is one of its quiet advantages.

["Use https so held requests and their data are encrypted","Authenticate each request with a token or session cookie, just like any API call","Authorize the cursor, so a user can only read updates they are allowed to see","Rate limit reconnections so a buggy or malicious client cannot hammer the server"]
items: Use https so held requests and their data are encrypted
Authenticate each request with a token or session cookie, just like any API call
Authorize the cursor, so a user can only read updates they are allowed to see
Rate limit reconnections so a buggy or malicious client cannot hammer the server

blocks.content: 12. Common Mistakes

["Forgetting the cursor, which silently drops events that occur in the gap between requests","Running it on a thread per request server, which exhausts threads under load","Setting no server timeout, so held requests pile up forever","Ignoring proxy timeouts that kill the connection before your own timeout fires","Using it for heavy two way traffic, where WebSockets are the better tool"]
items: Forgetting the cursor, which silently drops events that occur in the gap between requests
Running it on a thread per request server, which exhausts threads under load
Setting no server timeout, so held requests pile up forever
Ignoring proxy timeouts that kill the connection before your own timeout fires
Using it for heavy two way traffic, where WebSockets are the better tool

blocks.content: 13. HLD Interview: How to Talk About This
blocks.text: 13. HLD Interview: How to Talk About This

blocks.content: When asked to deliver updates without WebSockets, long polling is the answer to reach for.
Explain the mechanism: The client sends a request, the server holds it open until there is data, then responds, and the client immediately reconnects.
Contrast with short polling: Short polling wastes requests with empty responses, while long polling responds only when there is real data.
Call out the cursor: I track a last seen id so no update is lost in the gap between one response and the next request.
Address scaling: Because each client holds a connection, I use non blocking servers and make sure proxy and load balancer timeouts allow long lived requests.
